title: Reporting
subtitle: Reported speech, questions, commands and reporting verbs

blocks.text: If the reporting verb is in the past (e.g. **said**), we usually have to change the tense of what the person actually said. The general rule is go back one tense but there are some exceptions. With **past perfect simple** and **continuous**, there is no tense change.

rows.example: Sam **doesn't play** hockey very often. → Fiona said that Sam **didn't play** hockey very often.
**I'm winning!** → Carol shouted to us that she **was winning**.

rows.use: present perfect simple → past perfect simple
rows.example: **I've never been given** a trophy before. → Paul said that he'd **never been given** a trophy before.

rows.use: present perfect continuous → past perfect continuous
rows.example: **They've been playing** for four hours. → She told us that they'd **been playing** for four hours.
We **lost** the match. → Finally he told us that they **had lost** the match.
We **were winning** until half-time. → She said they **had been winning** until half-time.

blocks.text: When something is still true, we can change tense but we don't have to.
blocks.note: The article said that fishing **is/was** the most popular sport in Britain.

blocks.text: When we are reporting a scientific or historical fact, we don't usually change tense.
blocks.note: Alan told me that Queen Victoria **hated** Gladstone, the Prime Minister.

items: Although we can usually leave out **that** (Alan told me **(that)** Queen Victoria … ), we cannot leave out **that** after the verbs **reply** and **shout**.
I **replied that** going swimming in such cold water was a ridiculous idea.

theory.title: Reported speech: modal and semi-modal changes

blocks.text: If the reporting verb is in the past (e.g. **said**), we sometimes have to change modals and semi-modals. **Could, would, should, ought to, had better** and **need** do not change.

rows.example: 'I **could** swim when I was three,' said Lizzie. → Lizzie said that she **could** swim when she was three. (**could** does not change)
'I **can** swim 50 metres.' → She said she **could** swim 50 metres.

rows.use: must → must / had to / was to / should
rows.example: Obligation: **must** in direct speech usually changes to **had to, be to** or **should**.
'You **have to** train every day.' → He said we **had to** train every day.

rows.use: don't / doesn't have to → didn't have to
rows.example: 'You **don't have to** come.' → She said I **didn't have to** come.

rows.use: mustn't → mustn't / be not to / shouldn't
rows.example: When we are expressing obligation, **mustn't** can become **mustn't, be not to** or **shouldn't**.
'I **may** be late.' → He said he **might** be late.

rows.use: am / is / are going to → was / were going to
rows.example: 'I'm **going to** resign.' → She said she **was going to** resign.

blocks.text: When we are expressing obligation, **must** in direct speech usually changes to **had to, be to** or **should** in reported speech.
blocks.note: 'You **must** do what the referee tells you,' said the coach. → The coach said that we **had to / were to / should** do what the referee told us.

blocks.text: When we are expressing obligation, **mustn't** can become **mustn't, be not to** or **shouldn't**.
blocks.note: 'You **mustn't** cheat under any circumstances!' → We were told that we **mustn't / were not to / shouldn't** cheat under any circumstances.

blocks.text: **Must** doesn't usually change to **had to** or **should** when we are expressing probability.
blocks.note: 'It **must** have felt wonderful when they won!' said Dave. → Dave said that it **must** have felt wonderful when they won.

theory.title: Reported speech: pronoun and determiner changes

rows.example: It's **my** turn. → Eddie pointed out that it was **his** turn.
I bought **this** fishing rod yesterday. → Linda said she'd bought **the/that** fishing rod the day before.
**This** is a great game! → Tony said **it** was a great game.
Look at **these** baseball gloves! → Alison told us to look at **the** baseball gloves.
**These** are the best baseball gloves I've ever seen. → She said **they** were the best baseball gloves she'd ever seen.
I've had **these** for years. → She said she'd had **them** for years.

blocks.text: We do not need to change time words/phrases when the information is still true at the moment of speaking/writing.
blocks.note: 'I'll see you at the match next week,' said Dave. → Dave told us he'd see us at the match next week.

items: In narratives, writers often use direct speech time words and phrases for dramatic effect.
Carlo turned to Fraser and said that, **here, now**, they would decide who the champion was once and for all.

theory.title: Reported speech: time and place changes

rows.example: 'Come **here**.' → She told him to go **there**.

rows.use: tomorrow → the following / next day, the day after
rows.example: 'I'll call you **tomorrow**.' → He said he would call me **the following day**.
'See you **tonight**.' → She said she'd see us **that night**.

rows.use: yesterday → the day before, the previous day
rows.example: 'I saw her **yesterday**.' → He said he'd seen her **the day before**.

rows.use: now, at the moment → then, at that moment
rows.example: 'I'm busy **at the moment**.' → She said she was busy **at that moment**.

rows.use: next week / year / etc → the following / next week, the week after
rows.example: 'We're moving **next week**.' → They said they were moving **the following week**.

rows.use: last week / year / etc → the week before, the previous week
rows.example: 'I started **last year**.' → He said he'd started **the previous year**.
'I met her two days **ago**.' → She said she'd met her two days **before**.

blocks.text: With reported questions, we make the same changes regarding tense, pronoun and time and place words/phrases as we do with reported speech. In reported questions we don't use the question form or question marks.

rows.use: Questions beginning with have, do, be and modals
rows.example: '**Do** you want to play Monopoly?' asked Cheryl. → Cheryl asked **if/whether we wanted** to play Monopoly.

rows.use: Questions with what, who, which, when, where, why and how
rows.example: '**What time did** the match start?' asked Jimmy. → Jimmy asked Andrea **what time the match had started**.

blocks.text: The structure **question word + infinitive** is very common with reported questions.
blocks.note: She asked me **how to tune** a piano. · He asked me **what to do**.

rows.use: Commands · tell / command / order / instruct + sb + full infinitive
rows.example: 'Put the cricket bats away!' said Alex. → Alex **told me to put** the cricket bats away.
'Would you put the cricket bats away?' asked Alex. → Alex **asked me to put** the cricket bats away.

blocks.text: Different reporting verbs take different grammatical patterns. Some verbs can take more than one pattern, e.g. **deny doing, deny sth, deny (that)**.
